questions.question: What are table-driven tests in Go, and why are they the standard?
questions.title: Table Driven Tests
questions.direct_answer: A slice of test cases (input, expected) iterated with t.Run() — each case is a named subtest with its own PASS/FAIL. The standard because: one loop tests many cases, failures name the case, and adding a case is one line.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T[table of cases] --> LOOP[for each case]
    LOOP --> RUN[t.Run name]
    RUN --> PASS[subtest PASS]
    RUN --> FAIL[subtest FAIL: named]
    LOOP --> NEXT[next case]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The anonymous-struct idiom: the test-case struct is declared inline — it exists only for this table, and its fields document what the test data IS. For shared tables across tests, promote it to a named type.

The t.Run mechanics: each call creates a subtest with its own *testing.T — failures in one subtest don't stop the others (unless t.Fatal inside). The names form a path (TestDouble/negative) — the -run flag matches it (a regex over the full name).

The cleanup composable: t.Cleanup inside a t.Run registers per-subtest cleanup — each subtest gets its own setup/teardown through the same t that carries its lifetime. For shared setup, TestMain or t.Helper-wrapped init functions run once per package/test.

questions.direct_answer: Table Driven Tests is useful when it solves a clear problem in the code. sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
When debug a problem involving Table Driven Tests causes a problem, I reproduce it with the smallest input I can find.

I check the inputs and the expected result, trace the important state step by step, and add a test for the failure.

After the fix, I run the normal case and at least one edge case so the same bug does not return.

I avoid this by stating the assumption, handling the edge case, and adding a small test that would fail if the mistake returns.
